findings: At batch 1024, compiled BF16/FP16 with FP32 parameter/gradient/moment storage take 1.96861/1.97107 seconds per full update versus production control 2.85439 seconds: about 1.45x throughput or 31% less time. This includes the optimizer and input pipeline, unlike GPU-002's small-batch forward/backward diagnostic.

The matched FP32-storage BF16 fresh-only control takes 2.92994 seconds; adding BT4 compilation alone reduces this to 1.96861 seconds, about 33% less time. Changing storage alone is slightly slower here.

Compiled FP16 and BF16 are effectively tied in speed in this single allocation. FP16 has slightly lower common validation root/native CE (2.00734/1.46032) than BF16 (2.02385/1.46541) or production (2.02388/1.46533). These are one short run's descriptive losses, not strength or statistical superiority results.

Fused normalization backward takes 2.43727 seconds (14.6% less time); delayed prefetch alone takes 2.81140 seconds (1.5% less time); together 2.41963 seconds (15.2% less time). These arms retain original parameter/optimizer storage. Delaying prefetch shifts time from forward to backward and adds little net benefit here.

Disabling BT4 activation checkpointing in the compiled FP16 arm OOMed in the first backward pass: 41.34 GiB allocated, 2.22 GiB reserved/unallocated, failed 1 GiB allocation. Keep BT4 checkpointing on this L40S configuration; no batch-size reduction or allocator retry was performed.

The frozen fastest-eligible rule selected compiled BF16, whose tiny speed advantage over FP16 should not be interpreted as a meaningful ranking. Its separate-process update-545 to 550 replay reproduced exact model and optimizer/counter hashes and identical common validation. FP16's own fresh-process replay was not separately tested.

At the first step, 99.5088% of nonzero-gradient backbone coordinates retain unchanged stored values in production versus 1.6149% in FP32 storage. This is a quantization diagnostic proxy, not proof that every such coordinate had a nonzero intended update rounded away.

recommendation.runtime: Use regional BT4 compilation and retain BT4 activation checkpointing as the supported optimization direction. Treat FP32 parameter/moment storage as an explicit optimizer-state fork, never a transparent runtime change.
recommendation.precision: Compiled BF16 has the completed strict recovery proof. FP16 is effectively tied on speed and promising numerically/validation-wise, but requires its own recovery and deployment-policy checks before production selection.
recommendation.deferred: No CUDA Graphs, optimizer fusion, full epoch, search matches, Runpod rental, or automatic adoption. WSD child-contract support and verified expanded history data remain prerequisites to the requested long continuation.

limitations: All arms use the same already-materialized 50-update prefix, updates 501-550; this is within warmup. It does not test sustained peak LR under WSD or long-run stability.
One L40S allocation, fixed arm order, thirty warm measured updates 511-540; cold restore/compile, checkpoint I/O and validation excluded from warm timings and retained separately in records.

The harness uses existing training kernels/optimizer but separate orchestration and input/RNG hashing. No claim of bitwise equality to historical production runs; the first baseline loss differs from GPU-001 by about 2.34e-5.

Common validation is the first 1024 rows of HH-002's exposed 8128-position pool with eager BF16 compute for every arm; this is full-horizon/teacher-forced validation, not inference-aligned play or Elo.

FP32 storage promotes inherited BF16 values and moments exactly; it cannot recover precision already lost during the first 500 updates. It also changes subsequent optimizer arithmetic and cumulative learning.
